title: Houses and shelter: what keeps a home standing, dry and safe

summary.text: Push the top of a square frame sideways, and it leans over and folds flat. Push a triangle frame made of the same strips, and it keeps its shape. That is why roofs, towers and bridges are full of triangles. A shelter keeps us safe from rain, sun, heat, cold, wind and animals. People build it from what is close by: mud, bamboo, stone, grass, wood or brick. So a house in rainy Kerala has a steep tiled roof, and a house in dry Ladakh has a flat mud roof. New designs use less material and stand up better to floods and earthquakes. Safety rules keep builders and families from getting hurt.
summary.art: A row of Indian homes side by side: a Kerala house with a steep tiled roof, an Assam bamboo house on stilts, a Ladakh flat-roofed mud house, a round Kutch bhunga and a city block of flats, with a child's card frame shaped like a triangle in the front.

intro.hook: Make a square from four strips of card, joined at the corners with pins. Lay it flat and push one side gently. It leans over and squashes flat. Now make a triangle from three strips and push it the same way. Why does the triangle not lean?
intro.text: Every home has to stay standing. Wind pushes on it, its own heavy roof presses down on it, and sometimes the ground shakes. In this unit you test frames, roofs and tiles at home, and find out how builders all over India make houses that stand up, keep the rain out and keep people safe. You also meet houses made of mud, bamboo, stone and grass, and the people who are designing new ones.
intro.art: A child's hands on a table, one pressing a card square that has leaned into a flat diamond, the other pressing a card triangle that stays the same.

outcomes: I can say what a shelter does for people and for other living beings, and why homes differ from place to place.
I can build a square frame and a triangle frame, test them fairly, and explain why a triangle keeps its shape.
I can explain how one diagonal strip, called a brace, stops a frame leaning, and spot triangles in roofs, towers and bridges.
I can give examples of Indian houses built from natural materials, and say why each one suits its place.
I can explain why roofs slope, and why roof tiles must overlap with the upper tile on top.
I can name safety rules for building sites and for homes, and say why each rule matters.

terms.meaning: A place that protects a living being from rain, sun, heat, cold, wind and danger. A house is a shelter for people.
terms.example: A bus stop roof is a shelter when it rains. A crow's nest is a shelter for her eggs.
terms.art: People standing dry under a bus stop roof while rain falls around it.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of.
terms.example: A door can be made of wood, steel or plastic. Each one is a different material.
terms.art: Three doors side by side: wooden, steel and plastic.

terms.meaning: A material taken from nature and used with little change, such as mud, stone, bamboo, wood or grass.
terms.example: A Toda hut in the Nilgiris is made of bamboo, cane and thatch.
terms.art: A pile of mud, stones, bamboo poles and bundles of dry grass.

terms.meaning: The skeleton of a building: the poles, beams or strips that hold it up. Walls and roof are fixed onto the frame.
terms.example: A wedding pandal has a frame of poles tied with rope. The cloth is put on later.
terms.art: A pandal of tied poles with no cloth on it yet.

terms.meaning: The place where two parts of a frame meet and are fixed together.
terms.example: In your card frame, every pin is a joint.
terms.art: Close-up of two card strips held together by a brass split pin.

terms.meaning: Keeps its shape when it is pushed. A rigid frame does not lean or fold.
terms.example: Your card triangle is rigid. Your card square is not.
terms.art: A hand pushing a triangle that does not change, next to a square that leans.

terms.meaning: An extra strip or pole fixed from corner to corner across a frame, so that it cannot lean. A brace turns a square into two triangles.
terms.example: A wooden gate often has one diagonal plank across it. That plank is a brace.
terms.art: A wooden gate with a diagonal plank from one corner to the opposite corner.

terms.meaning: A frame made of many triangles joined together. It is strong but uses little material.
terms.example: Many roofs, mobile phone towers and railway bridges are trusses.
terms.art: A steel railway bridge whose sides are a long row of triangles.

terms.meaning: The weight or push that a building or frame has to hold up.
terms.example: A roof's load is its own weight, plus rain, and people or water tanks on top.
terms.art: A flat roof with a water tank on it and arrows pointing down.

terms.meaning: How steeply a surface tilts. A steep slope is high at one end and low at the other.
terms.example: Rain runs off a steep roof quickly. On a flat roof it can stand in puddles.
terms.art: Two roofs, one steep and one nearly flat, with rain running off the steep one.

terms.meaning: A roof made of thick layers of dry grass, straw, reeds or palm leaves.
terms.example: Some village houses in Tamil Nadu and Kerala have thatch made of dried coconut leaves.
terms.art: A small house with a thick roof of dried coconut leaves.

terms.meaning: A sudden shaking of the ground, caused by huge blocks of rock deep under the ground slipping past each other.
terms.example: In January 2001, a big earthquake shook Kutch in Gujarat.
terms.art: A cracked road and a gently shaking house, with wavy lines under the ground.

explanations.definition: A shelter is a place that protects a living being from the weather and from danger, so they can rest, sleep and keep their young and their food safe.
explanations.description: Shelter is one of our basic needs, along with air, water, food and clothing. A house keeps off rain and sun, keeps out cold wind, and keeps out snakes, rats and thieves. People are not the only ones who build shelters. A male baya weaver bird weaves a hanging nest of grass strips. His problem is that snakes and other hunters eat eggs and chicks. So the nest hangs from a thin branch, often over water, and the way in is a long tube that opens downwards. A hunter finds it very hard to reach inside. Ants dig rooms under the ground, where it stays cool and damp. A shelter must suit the weather of its place and the life of whoever lives in it.
examples: A city flat keeps a family dry in the monsoon and cool in summer.
A baya weaver's nest hangs over water, with its door at the bottom.
Ants keep their eggs in rooms under the soil, out of the hot sun.
explanations.art: A baya weaver nest hanging from a thin branch over a pond, with a long entrance tube at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card says what a shelter is for, and shows that birds and ants build shelters too.

explanations.concept: Why a triangle keeps its shape
explanations.definition: A triangle frame is rigid: it cannot change shape unless one of its sides gets longer, shorter or breaks. A square frame can lean over without any side changing length.
explanations.description: Join three strips into a triangle. Once the three lengths are fixed, there is only one shape they can make. To lean, one strip would have to stretch or squash, and strong strips do not. Join four strips into a square, and the corners can turn like hinges. The square leans into a diamond and then folds flat, though every strip stays the same length. Add one strip from one corner to the opposite corner. Now the square is two triangles, and it is rigid. That extra strip is called a brace. A frame made of many triangles is called a truss. Builders use trusses in roofs, towers, cranes and bridges, because they hold a big load with little material.
examples: A roof of a shed or a factory is often held up by wooden or steel triangles.
A mobile phone tower is a tall truss made of steel triangles.
The Howrah Bridge in Kolkata is a steel bridge made of many triangles.
explanations.art: Three card frames side by side: a square leaning into a diamond, a square with one diagonal strip staying square, and a triangle staying the same.
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the Push Test: why the square leaned and the triangle did not.

explanations.concept: Houses are built from what is near
explanations.definition: Long ago, people built homes from materials found close by. The weather of the place decided what kind of house kept people safe and comfortable.
explanations.description: Carrying heavy materials far is hard, so people used what they had. In Kerala and coastal Karnataka, many old houses have walls of laterite, a reddish stone cut from the ground, and steep roofs of clay tiles for the heavy monsoon rain. In Assam, some families, such as the Mising people, build bamboo houses raised on poles. When the river floods, the water flows under the floor. In Ladakh, rain and snow are light, so houses have thick walls of sun-dried mud bricks and flat mud roofs. Thick mud walls are slow to heat up in the day and slow to cool at night. In the Nilgiris, the Toda people built small huts with a rounded roof of bamboo, cane and thatch. In Kutch, round mud houses called bhungas have light cone-shaped roofs. Today many homes are made of brick, cement, steel and glass, which can be carried a long way by truck.
examples: A Kerala house with a steep tiled roof.
A Mising house on bamboo stilts in Assam.
A flat-roofed mud house in Ladakh.
A round bhunga with a cone roof in Kutch, Gujarat.
explanations.art: A map of India with five small houses drawn on it: Kerala, Assam, Ladakh, the Nilgiris and Kutch.
explanations.context: This card is about why homes in different parts of India look so different.

explanations.definition: A sloping roof lets rain run off before it can soak in or leak. Roof tiles overlap, with each higher tile lying on top of the one below it, so water always runs onto the outside of the next tile.
explanations.description: Water flows downhill. On a flat roof it can stand in puddles and slowly find its way through cracks. On a steep roof it runs off in seconds. That is why places with very heavy rain, like Kerala, the Konkan coast and the north-east, have steep roofs. Places with little rain, like Ladakh and much of Rajasthan, often have flat roofs, which people also use for drying grain and sleeping on hot nights. Tiles must overlap the right way. If the higher tile lies on top of the lower one, water runs from one tile onto the next and off the edge. If the lower tile lies on top, water runs into the gap and drips inside. Mangalore tiles, made in Mangaluru since the 1860s, have grooves that lock each tile to its neighbours.
examples: Steep tiled roofs in Kerala villages.
Flat mud roofs in Ladakh, used for drying apricots and storing hay.
The tin sheet over a balcony slopes outwards, so rain falls off the edge.
explanations.art: A side view of roof tiles overlapping, upper over lower, with blue arrows of rain running from tile to tile and off the edge.
explanations.context: This card explains your roof tests: why roofs slope and which way tiles must overlap.

explanations.definition: Weight pushes a building down, but wind and earthquakes push it sideways. A building stays up in an earthquake if its frame cannot lean and its heavy parts cannot fall.
explanations.description: Most walls are good at holding weight that presses straight down. A sideways push is harder. It is like your push on the card square. Builders stop this in three main ways. They add braces and triangles, so the frame cannot lean. They tie walls together with bands of concrete or wood, so the walls move as one piece. And they keep roofs light, because a heavy roof that falls is the most dangerous part. In the Kutch earthquake of 26 January 2001, many round bhungas with light roofs in the Banni area were reported to have stood, while many newer buildings fell. Round walls have no long flat side for the shaking to push over. A badly built concrete building can be more dangerous than a well-built mud one.
examples: Tall buildings have braces, or a very stiff central core, to stand up to wind.
Engineers test model buildings on shaking tables before building real ones.
Rules for building in earthquake areas ask for bands of concrete tying the walls together.
explanations.art: A small model house on a tray being shaken, with sideways arrows, and a diagonal brace inside its walls.
explanations.context: This card explains why sideways pushes from wind and earthquakes are the hardest for a house.

explanations.concept: New designs: less material, more comfort
explanations.description: People keep inventing new ways to build. Laurie Baker, an architect born in England who made his home in Kerala, built with local brick and stone. His rat-trap bond lays bricks on their edges, with an air gap inside the wall. It uses about a quarter fewer bricks and keeps rooms cooler. His jaali walls, with holes between the bricks, let breeze through. Other builders prefer concrete and steel, which are strong, quick to build tall, and easy to find. People still argue about which is better, because the answer depends on the place, the money, the weather and how well the house is built.
examples: Brick walls with gaps in a pattern, called jaali, in many Laurie Baker buildings in Thiruvananthapuram.
Tall blocks of concrete flats in Chennai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.
Houses built with blocks of pressed mud and a little cement, made near the building site.

perspectives.who: An architect who builds with mud and brick
perspectives.explanation: Local mud and brick cost less, need little energy to make, and keep rooms cool without a fan or AC. A well-made mud wall can last a hundred years.

perspectives.who: A builder who builds with concrete
perspectives.explanation: Concrete with steel rods inside is very strong and can be built many floors high, which a crowded city needs. It does not wash away in heavy rain.
The material matters less than how well it is built. Braces, bands that tie the walls, and a light roof save more lives than any one material.

explanations.art: A brick wall with a pattern of gaps letting sunlight and breeze through into a cool room.
explanations.context: This card is about new designs for homes, and a real argument about which materials are best.

explanations.concept: Safety rules when building and at home
explanations.definition: Safety rules are steps that stop people getting hurt. On a building site and at home, most injuries come from falls, falling objects, sharp tools and electricity.
explanations.description: Builders wear a hard helmet, because a falling brick or tool can hurt the head. They wear strong shoes, because nails and broken glass lie on the ground. Workers high up wear a harness tied to the building, so a slip does not become a fall. Bright jackets help drivers of trucks and cranes see them. At home, the same dangers are smaller but real. Children do not climb on balcony walls, grills or water tanks. Wet floors are wiped at once. Broken switches and loose wires are left for a grown-up to fix. In this unit, a grown-up does every step with a sharp point, a knife or a hammer.
examples: A worker on scaffolding wearing a yellow helmet and a harness.
A sign at a building site saying 'Helmets must be worn'.
Grills or a net on a high balcony so that nobody can fall.
explanations.art: A woman builder on a site wearing a yellow helmet, strong boots and a bright orange jacket, carrying bricks.
explanations.context: This card lists the main safety rules for building, and why each one matters.

agreed.text: A triangle frame keeps its shape when pushed. A square frame leans unless it has a brace.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with card strips and pins, as in the Push Test. Engineers have used this in bridges and roofs for hundreds of years.

agreed.text: Sloping roofs shed rain faster than flat roofs.
agreed.evidence: Water flows downhill. You can see it on the tray roof in the Rain on the Roof test, and in every monsoon.

agreed.text: Traditional houses often suit their weather well, because people improved them over many generations.
agreed.evidence: Studies of mud houses in hot, dry places show their thick walls keep rooms cooler in the day than thin walls do.

agreed.text: Most deaths in earthquakes are caused by buildings falling, not by the shaking itself.
agreed.evidence: Reports after earthquakes all over the world, including Latur in 1993 and Kutch in 2001, show this.

challenging.claim: A square is stronger than a triangle, because it has more sides.
challenging.who: A common first guess among children and many grown-ups
challenging.for: Four strips use more material than three, so it seems they should be stronger.
challenging.against: In the Push Test, the square leans and folds flat with a gentle push. The triangle does not, because three fixed sides allow only one shape.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common guess: that more sides make a stronger frame.

challenging.claim: Concrete houses are always safer than mud houses.
challenging.for: Concrete with steel rods inside is very strong, and does not wash away in rain.
challenging.against: In the 2001 Kutch earthquake, many newer buildings fell while many old bhungas stood. A badly built concrete house with a heavy roof can be more dangerous than a well-built mud one.
challenging.context: This card is about whether one material is always the safest.

challenging.claim: Thick, heavy walls and roofs make a house safe in an earthquake.
challenging.who: An old belief in many places
challenging.for: Heavy walls feel solid and are hard to push over by hand.
challenging.against: In the Latur earthquake in Maharashtra in 1993, many heavy stone walls and roofs fell on people asleep at night. A shaking ground pushes heavy things harder, so heavy roofs are more dangerous.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that heavier means safer.

challenging.claim: Mud houses are old-fashioned and only for the poor.
challenging.who: Many people in towns and cities
challenging.for: Most new houses in cities are made of concrete, and mud walls need care after heavy rain.
challenging.against: Mud is cheap, cool in summer, and can be used again. Architects in India and around the world now build new mud houses on purpose, for families who can afford anything.
challenging.context: This card is about whether mud houses belong only to the past.

big_questions.q: A triangle stays rigid and a square leans. Why does having one more side make a frame weaker, not stronger?
big_questions.hint: Push the corners of your square. Which parts turn? Do the strips get longer or shorter, or only the corners?

big_questions.q: Your body has a skeleton, like a house has a frame. Where in your body are there triangles?
big_questions.hint: Stand with your feet apart and look at your legs and the floor. Look at your arm when you put your hand on your hip.

big_questions.q: A bird, an ant and a person all build shelters. Is a nest a home in the same way a house is?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one is for: sleeping, keeping young safe, keeping food, being together.

big_questions.q: A house is walls around an empty space. Which part do we live in: the walls or the space?
big_questions.hint: Think about a room with no door or window, and a room with no walls at all.

big_questions.q: If people everywhere build with concrete and glass, will all cities start to look the same? Does that matter?
big_questions.hint: Think about the weather in Chennai and in Shimla. Should their houses be the same?

story.title: The Pandal That Leaned
story.note: Pandals of casuarina poles tied with coir rope are really built for weddings and festivals in Tamil Nadu. Meenakshi, Selvi, Arun and this wedding are made up.
text: Meenakshi was nine, and her cousin Lakshmi was getting married on Sunday. The wedding lunch would be on the terrace of Paati's house in Madurai. On Thursday morning, a lorry brought a load of long, thin casuarina poles and bundles of coir rope.

Selvi Athai, Meenakshi's aunt, built pandals for a living. A pandal is a big shade of cloth held up on a frame of poles. Selvi Athai had built pandals for temple festivals, school sports days and hundreds of weddings. This time she said her son Arun could build the frame himself. Arun was twelve. He had watched his mother work since he was small.

Arun worked hard all day. He stood the poles up in rows, each one in a heavy pot of sand. He tied long poles across the top, from post to post, with tight coir knots. By evening the frame stood on the terrace like a big grid of squares. Meenakshi carried rope and water and held the ladder.
"Not bad," said Arun, wiping his face. "Tomorrow we put the cloth on."
That night the wind came. It was the end of the monsoon, and the wind blew hard across the terraces. Meenakshi woke up and heard the poles creaking. She ran upstairs in her nightie.

The whole frame was leaning. Every pole had tipped the same way, like a row of people pushed by a crowd. The squares between the poles had become long, thin diamonds. Not one knot had come undone. Not one pole had broken. But the pandal was leaning over towards the edge of the terrace.
Arun came up behind her. "Amma!" he shouted down the stairs. "Come quickly!"
Selvi Athai came up with a torch. She did not shout. She walked once round the frame and pushed one pole with her hand. The whole frame swayed.
"Your knots are good," she said to Arun. "Your poles are good. Something is missing. Meenakshi, give me four of those short sticks from the broom."

Meenakshi pulled four thin sticks out of the coconut broom. Selvi Athai tied them at the ends with thread to make a small square. She put the little square on the floor and pushed one corner with her finger. It leaned and fell flat, just like the pandal.
Then she took three sticks and tied them into a triangle. "Push this one," she said.
Meenakshi pushed. She pushed harder. The triangle slid across the floor, but it did not change shape at all.
"Why doesn't it lean?" asked Arun.
"Try to make it lean," said his mother. "Which stick has to change?"

Meenakshi looked at it for a long time. "To lean, one stick would have to get longer, or shorter," she said slowly. "And the sticks can't. But in the square, none of the sticks has to change. Only the corners turn."

"That's it," said Selvi Athai. She tied one more broom stick across the little square, from one corner to the opposite corner. Now there were two triangles inside the square. Meenakshi pushed it. It did not lean.
Arun's face went red. "I forgot the cross poles," he said. "I've seen you tie them a hundred times. I thought they were just for hanging lights."
"Everyone forgets something on their first pandal," said Selvi Athai. "I forgot the cross poles on mine, too. My mother made me take the whole thing down."

They worked until the wind dropped. Selvi Athai held the torch. Arun climbed the ladder. Meenakshi passed up rope. At each end of the pandal, and in the middle, they tied a long pole from the top of one post down to the foot of the next. Every one made a triangle. As each pole was tied, the frame stood a little straighter. By the time the sky turned grey, the pandal stood upright, and the wind could not move it.

On Sunday, the pandal was covered in white cloth and strings of jasmine and marigold. Two hundred guests ate sambar, rice and payasam on banana leaves underneath it. Nobody looked at the cross poles. They were hidden behind the cloth.
But Meenakshi knew they were there. After lunch she found Arun on the stairs, eating a third laddu.
"Next year," she said, "I'm building one."
"You'll need cross poles," said Arun.
"I know," said Meenakshi. "I'll need triangles."
story.epiphany: A frame of squares can lean even when every knot and pole is strong, because its corners can turn. A triangle cannot lean unless one of its sides changes length. So one cross pole, which turns a square into two triangles, keeps the whole pandal upright.
ask: No knot came undone and no pole broke. So why did the pandal lean?
How did the little square of broom sticks help Meenakshi understand the big pandal?
Why did the triangle slide across the floor without changing shape?
Arun thought the cross poles were only for hanging lights. Why do people sometimes copy what they see without knowing why it is done?
Where in your home or street could you add a cross piece to stop something wobbling?

experiments.title: The Push Test: square frame or triangle frame?
experiments.context: This is the main investigation of the unit. You build three frames from card strips: a square, a triangle, and a square with one strip across it. Then you push each one sideways and measure how far it leans.
experiments.question: When we push the top of a frame sideways, which shape keeps its shape best: a square, a triangle, or a square with one strip from corner to corner?
experiments.predict: Look at the strips. A square uses four strips and a triangle uses only three. Which frame do you think will lean the most when you push it? Which will lean the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same kind of strips, the same pins and the same push for every frame. Only the shape changes. Hold the bottom strip still each time. Push each frame 3 times, because one push can be a fluke.

Push 1: how far the top corner moved (cm)
Did it fold flat? (yes or no)

materials.item: an empty cereal, biscuit or shoe box, cut into flat strips of card 2 cm wide and 15 cm long
one longer card strip, 2 cm wide and 25 cm long, for the brace
brass split pins, also called paper fasteners. No split pins? Push a short twist tie from a bread packet through the holes and twist it, or tie a thread through and knot it on both sides.
a ruler with centimetres
cello tape
a sharp pencil or the point of a geometry-box compass, and an eraser to press on, for making holes

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes with the compass point or a sharp pencil, pressing the card onto an eraser. Keep split pins away from babies, who may swallow them.

schedule.what: Make the strips and frames. Guess. Push each frame three times and measure. Say what you found and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the three frames, before and after the push, and write one sentence under each drawing.

setup.art: Card strips 2 cm wide cut from a cereal box, each with a small hole 1 cm from each end, and a few brass split pins.
setup.caption: 1. Cut strips and make a hole near each end.

setup.art: Three card frames on a table: a square of four strips, a triangle of three strips, and a square with one long strip from corner to corner.
setup.caption: 2. Join the strips with split pins into three frames.

setup.art: A frame lying flat on a table with its bottom strip taped down, a ruler beside the top strip, and a finger pushing the top strip sideways.
setup.caption: 3. Tape the bottom strip down. Push the top sideways and measure.

flow.do: 1. Cut 7 card strips, each 2 cm wide and 15 cm long. 2. Cut one strip 25 cm long. 3. Make a hole 1 cm from each end of the short strips.
flow.say: We are going to build three frames, like the skeletons of tiny houses. First we need strips. I will make the holes with the compass point.
flow.kid: Help cut strips of card. Each one is 2 cm wide and 15 cm long. A grown-up makes a hole near each end.
flow.parent: Press the card onto an eraser and twist the compass point to make each hole. The holes should be a little loose round the pin, so the corners can turn. Cereal box card works well. Thin paper is too floppy.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Push Test. Here you make the card strips for three frames.

flow.do: 1. Join four strips into a square, with a split pin at each corner. 2. Join the other three strips into a triangle. 3. Keep the long strip for later.
flow.say: Let's join the strips. Push a split pin through two holes and open its legs flat at the back. Make a square, then a triangle.
flow.kid: Join four strips into a square with split pins. Then join three strips into a triangle.
flow.parent: Open the pin's legs flat, but do not press the joint tight. The corners should be able to turn freely, like a hinge. If you used twist ties or thread, keep them loose too.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the square and the triangle. 2. Ask your child which one will lean more when pushed. 3. Write the guess and the reason in the table.
flow.say: The square has four strips and the triangle has only three. When I push the top sideways, which one will lean more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the square and the triangle. Which will lean more when you push it? Why? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think that one will lean less?
good: The square has more strips, so it is stronger.
The triangle has a pointed top, so it is harder to push.
I don't know, let's test it.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Many children guess the square is stronger because it has more strips. That is a fine guess. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Lay the square flat on the table. 2. Tape its bottom strip down firmly. 3. Lay the ruler beside the top strip, with 0 at the top left corner. 4. Push the top strip sideways with one finger, gently. 5. Read how far the corner moved.
flow.say: Push the top strip sideways, about as hard as you press a doorbell. Watch the ruler. How many centimetres did the corner move?
flow.kid: Tape the bottom strip down. Push the top strip sideways, gently. Read the ruler. How far did the corner move?
flow.parent: The square will lean into a diamond and keep going until it is almost flat. The corner usually moves 10 to 14 cm. Lift it back to a square before each push. Write all three pushes.

flow.do: 1. Untape the square. 2. Tape the triangle's bottom strip down. 3. Push the top corner sideways in the same way, three times. 4. Measure each time.
flow.say: Now the triangle. Same push, same ruler. Watch the corner closely.
flow.kid: Now push the triangle the same way, three times. Measure how far the corner moves.
flow.parent: The triangle's top corner should move less than 1 cm, only as much as the loose holes allow. If the card bends, use thicker card. A triangle that slides across the table needs its bottom strip taped more firmly.

check.q: When you pushed the triangle, why did it not lean like the square?
options: It was made of stronger card
To lean, one of its sides would have to get longer or shorter
It had fewer pins, so it was lighter
check.why: Both frames used the same card and the same pins. A triangle with three fixed sides can only make one shape. To lean, a side would have to stretch or squash. A square can lean just by turning its corners, with no side changing length.

flow.do: 1. Put the square back together as a square. 2. Lay the long strip from the bottom left corner to the top right corner. 3. Mark where it crosses the top right pin. 4. A grown-up makes a hole there and pins it on.
flow.say: What if we add one strip across the square, from corner to corner? Guess first: will it still lean?
flow.kid: Add the long strip across the square, from one corner to the opposite corner. Will it lean now? Guess first.
flow.parent: Hold the square straight while you mark the second hole, so the brace fits exactly. The long strip shares a pin at each of its two corners.

flow.do: Push the braced square three times, the same way, and measure.
flow.say: Same push again. How far does the corner move now?
flow.kid: Push the square with the long strip. Measure how far it moves.
flow.parent: It should now move less than 1 cm, like the triangle. The long strip has turned the square into two triangles. This strip is called a brace.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think now, what I saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.

ask.q: Why did the square fold, though no strip got longer or shorter?
good: Because the corners turned like hinges.
Because a square can change shape without changing its sides.

flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A strong answer names the shape, gives the numbers from the table, and says that the triangle's sides cannot change length.
flow.think: Look at a gate, a chair or a ladder at home. Can you find a brace that turns a square into triangles?

experiments.title: Rain on the Roof: how steep should it be?
experiments.context: In this test you make a model roof from a tray or a plastic file. You pour the same amount of water on it at three slopes, and time how long it takes to run off.
experiments.question: Does water run off a steep roof faster than a flat one, and does any water stay behind on a flat roof?
experiments.predict: We will pour water on a roof that is flat, a little tilted and very tilted. Which roof will be dry first? Will any water stay on the flat one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same roof, the same 4 spoons of water and the same pouring place each time. Only the slope changes. Wipe the roof dry between tries. Do each slope twice.
results_table: My guess: seconds to stop dripping
Water left in puddles? (yes or no)

materials.item: a flat plastic tray, a plastic file cover, or a steel plate with no rim, as the roof
books of about the same thickness, to lift one end
a tablespoon and a cup of water
a bowl or a cloth to catch water at the low end
a phone stopwatch or a clock with a seconds hand

experiments.safety: Wipe up spilled water at once, so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Pour 4 spoons of water on a flat, a low and a steep roof. Time how long until it stops dripping.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three roofs and colour any puddles left on them.

setup.art: A plastic tray lying flat on a table, a spoon pouring water onto its middle, a bowl at one edge.
setup.caption: 1. Pour 4 spoons of water on the flat roof.

setup.art: The same tray with one end lifted on one book, water running towards a bowl at the low end.
setup.caption: 2. Lift one end on one book and pour again.

setup.art: The same tray lifted on four books, water running off fast into the bowl, a stopwatch beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Lift it on four books. Time until the dripping stops.

flow.do: 1. Lay the tray flat on a table, with one edge over a bowl. 2. Show the cup of water and the spoon.
flow.say: This tray is our roof. Rain falls on it. Where will the water go if the roof is flat? Where will it go if we tilt it?
flow.kid: The tray is a roof. Will rain run off a flat roof? What about a tilted one?
flow.context: This is the first step of Rain on the Roof. Here you set up a tray as a model roof.

flow.do: Ask for a guess for each slope: flat, one book and four books. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Which roof will be dry first? Will any water stay on the flat roof? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which roof will be dry first. Will water stay on the flat one? Why?
flow.parent: Accept any guess with a reason. Do not explain yet.

flow.do: 1. Pour 4 spoons of water onto the middle of the flat tray. 2. Start the stopwatch. 3. Stop it when no drop has fallen for 5 seconds, or after 60 seconds. 4. Wipe dry. 5. Repeat with one book, then four books.
flow.say: Pour slowly, all in the same place. Start the clock now. Tell me when the drips stop.
flow.kid: Pour 4 spoons in the middle. Start the clock. Stop it when the drips stop.
flow.parent: On the flat tray, most water stays in a puddle, so write 'more than 60' and 'yes'. On one book, water creeps slowly and some drops stay behind. On four books, it runs off in a few seconds. Do each slope twice.

flow.do: Look at the results together and talk about where houses have steep roofs.
flow.say: Kerala gets very heavy rain in the monsoon. Ladakh gets very little. Which roof would you build in each place? Why?
flow.kid: Kerala gets lots of rain. Ladakh gets very little. Which roof suits each place?

check.q: Why do many old houses in Kerala have steep roofs?
options: Steep roofs are easier to climb on
Rain runs off a steep roof quickly, before it can soak in or leak
Steep roofs keep out the sun better
check.why: On your steep tray, water ran off in seconds. On the flat tray, it stayed in a puddle. In heavy monsoon rain, a steep roof sheds water before it can soak in or leak through cracks.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think now, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you think now. Say what you saw. Say why.
flow.parent: A strong answer gives the times, says water flows downhill, and links steep roofs to places with heavy rain.

experiments.title: Which Way Should the Tiles Overlap?
experiments.context: In this test you make two small model roofs of plastic tiles cut from milk packets. On one, each higher tile lies on top of the one below. On the other, each lower tile lies on top. A tissue underneath shows where water leaks through.
experiments.question: Does it matter which way roof tiles overlap? Which way keeps the tissue underneath dry?
experiments.predict: On roof A, each higher tile lies on top of the tile below it. On roof B, each lower tile lies on top of the tile above it. Which roof will keep the tissue dry? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same tiles, the same slope and the same 4 spoons of water for both roofs. Only the way the tiles overlap changes. Do each roof twice, with a fresh dry tissue.
results_table: My guess: will the tissue get wet?
Try 1: wet spots on the tissue
Try 2: wet spots on the tissue

materials.item: two clean, empty milk packets, cut into 8 rectangles of plastic, each about 6 cm by 10 cm. Any thin plastic bag works too.
two pieces of card, each about 12 cm by 20 cm, as the roof base
cello tape
two paper tissues or sheets of newspaper, to lay under the roofs
a few books to tilt the roofs, and a tablespoon of water

experiments.safety: Wash the milk packets and dry them before cutting. A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Make two tiled roofs that overlap different ways. Pour water on each. Look for wet spots on the tissue below.

experiments.record: Draw a side view of both roofs, with arrows showing where the water went. Mark where the tissue got wet.

setup.art: Four plastic rectangles taped in rows on a card, each higher one lying over the top edge of the one below, like real roof tiles.
setup.caption: 1. Roof A: each higher tile lies on top of the one below.

setup.art: Four plastic rectangles taped in rows on a card, each lower one lying over the bottom edge of the one above.
setup.caption: 2. Roof B: each lower tile lies on top of the one above.

setup.art: Both roofs tilted on books over tissues, a spoon pouring water at the top, and wet spots showing on one tissue only.
setup.caption: 3. Tilt both roofs over tissues and pour water at the top.

flow.do: 1. Cut a slit 3 cm wide down the middle of each card, from just below the top to just above the bottom. 2. Tape 4 plastic tiles in rows across each card, covering the slit.
flow.say: The slit in the card is like the gaps in a real roof. If water gets through the tiles, it will drip through the slit onto the tissue.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a slit in each card. Tape 4 plastic tiles over the slit.
flow.parent: On roof A, start taping at the bottom: tape the lowest tile first, then lay each higher tile so it covers the top 2 cm of the one below. On roof B, start at the top, so each lower tile covers the bottom 2 cm of the one above. Tape each tile along its two side edges only, so water can run over or under the tile edges.
flow.context: This is the first step of the tile test. Here you build two model roofs whose tiles overlap in opposite ways.

flow.do: Show both roofs side by side and ask for a guess.
flow.say: Look at the edges of the tiles on each roof. When water runs down, which roof will let it in? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at both roofs. Which one will let water through? Why?
flow.parent: Ask your child to run a finger down each roof, from top to bottom. On roof B the finger catches on each tile edge. That is where water gets caught too.

flow.do: 1. Tilt each roof on two books over a dry tissue. 2. Pour 4 spoons of water slowly along the top edge. 3. Lift the roof and look at the tissue. 4. Repeat with fresh tissues.
flow.say: Pour slowly along the top. Now lift the roof. Is the tissue wet? Where?
flow.kid: Tilt each roof over a tissue. Pour water along the top. Lift it up. Is the tissue wet?
flow.parent: Under roof A the tissue should stay dry, because water runs from the top of each tile onto the outside of the next. Under roof B, water runs into the edge of each tile, under it, and through the slit. You should see wet spots.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think now, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me what you think now, what you saw, and why the water went where it did.
flow.kid: Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why.

check.q: On a real roof, how must the tiles overlap to keep the rain out?
options: Each higher tile lies on top of the tile below it
Each lower tile lies on top of the tile above it
It does not matter, as long as there are no gaps
check.why: Water runs downhill. If each higher tile covers the top of the one below, water runs off one tile onto the outside of the next and never reaches an edge it can slip under. Roof B let water into every edge, and your tissue got wet.

activities.title: What Is Our Home Made Of? A home walk
activities.context: This is a short walk round your own home. You look at walls, floor, roof, doors and windows, and name the material each one is made of and why.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Look at the balcony from inside, and don't climb on anything to see the roof.

schedule.what: Walk round the home. Name the material of each part, and why it was chosen.

activities.record: Make a table: part of the house, material, and why that material.

setup.art: A child and a mother walking through a flat, the child pointing at a window, the mother holding a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round your home with a notebook.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table: window, glass, lets light in; door, wood, strong and can be locked; floor, tiles, easy to clean.
setup.caption: 2. Write each part, its material, and why.

flow.do: 1. Walk to the main door, a window, the floor, a wall and the ceiling. 2. At each one, ask what it is made of. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: Let's be detectives in our own home. What is this door made of? Why do you think the builder chose that?
flow.kid: Look at the door, a window, the floor and a wall. What is each made of? Why?

ask.q: Why is the window made of glass, not wood?

flow.parent: Walls in most flats are brick or concrete blocks, covered with cement plaster and paint. Floors are often tiles, stone or concrete. Under the plaster, a concrete roof has steel rods inside.
flow.context: This is a home walk. Here you name what each part of your home is made of.

flow.do: Ask which materials came from nature with little change, and which were made in a factory.
flow.say: Which of these came from nature, like wood or stone? Which were made in a factory, like glass or cement?
flow.kid: Which materials came from nature? Which were made in a factory?
flow.parent: Wood and stone come from nature. Glass is made from sand, and cement from limestone and clay, but both are heated in factories. Every material started in nature.

activities.title: Triangle Hunt
activities.context: After the Push Test, you hunt for triangles that hold things up: at home, from the window, and in photos of bridges and towers.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a phone or book with photos of a bridge, a crane or a mobile tower, if you can't see one from home

activities.safety: Look from inside a window or a balcony with a grill. Never lean over a balcony wall.

schedule.what: Find and draw five triangles that hold something up.

activities.record: Draw five triangles you found. Under each, write what it holds up.

setup.art: A child at a grilled window pointing at a mobile phone tower made of steel triangles on a building across the road.
setup.caption: 1. Look out of the window for towers, cranes and roofs.

setup.art: A folding wooden stool and an ironing board at home, with their triangles outlined in red.
setup.caption: 2. Look at home: stools, stands, shelves and ladders.

flow.do: 1. Look at stools, a cloth-drying stand, shelf brackets, a ladder and the ironing board. 2. Look out of the window at towers, cranes and roofs. 3. Draw each triangle you find.
flow.say: Remember how the triangle frame would not lean? Builders know that too. Let's find triangles that are holding something up.
flow.kid: Find triangles that hold something up. Look at home and out of the window. Draw them.
flow.parent: Good finds: the bracket under a shelf, the legs of a folding stand, a ladder leaning on a wall with the floor, a mobile tower, a crane, the steel roof of a bus stand or a railway station.
flow.context: This is the Triangle Hunt. Here you find triangles that keep real things from leaning.

flow.do: Look at photos of the Howrah Bridge in Kolkata, or a railway bridge near you. Count the triangles on one side.
flow.say: This is the Howrah Bridge in Kolkata. Its sides are made of steel triangles. Why do you think the builders used so many?
flow.kid: Look at a photo of a steel bridge. Count the triangles. Why so many?

check.q: Why does a steel bridge have triangles along its sides?
options: They look nice
Triangles keep their shape, so the bridge does not lean or sag
Triangles let the wind through
check.why: A triangle cannot change shape unless a side changes length. So a bridge made of triangles stays firm under heavy trains and in the wind, and uses less steel than a solid wall would. The wind does pass through the gaps, which also helps, but the main reason is that triangles stay firm.

activities.title: Homes of India: match the house to the place
activities.context: In this activity you match pictures of houses from different parts of India to their place, and give a reason from the weather.

materials.item: the printed house cards and place cards from this unit, or a sheet of paper to draw them

schedule.what: Match six houses to six places. Give a reason for each from the weather or the land.

activities.record: Stick or draw each house next to its place, with one reason.

setup.art: Six house cards on a table: a steep tiled Kerala house, a bamboo house on stilts, a flat-roofed mud house, a round cone-roofed hut, a half-barrel thatch hut, and a block of flats.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the six house cards.

setup.art: Six place cards beside them: Kerala, Assam, Ladakh, Kutch, the Nilgiris and Chennai, each with a small weather picture.
setup.caption: 2. Match each house to a place, and give a reason.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the house cards and the place cards. 2. Ask your child to match them. 3. Ask for a reason each time.
flow.say: Each of these homes suits its place. Which one is from the place with floods? Which is from the cold desert? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Match each house to a place. Give a reason each time.
flow.parent: Kerala: steep tiled roof, heavy rain. Assam: bamboo house on stilts, floods. Ladakh: flat mud roof and thick mud walls, very little rain and cold nights. Kutch: round bhunga with a light roof, earthquakes and heat. Nilgiris: the Toda hut with a rounded thatch roof, cool hills. Chennai: a block of flats, many people and little land.
flow.context: This is a matching activity. Here you match Indian houses to the places they come from.

flow.do: Ask why a family in a city lives in a block of flats.
flow.say: Why do so many families in Chennai live in tall blocks of flats? What does a city have too little of?
flow.kid: Why do city families often live in flats, one on top of another?
flow.parent: A city has many people and little land. Building upwards gives many homes on one small piece of land.

activities.title: Safety Walk: find the dangers at home
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home with a grown-up and look for places where someone could get hurt. Then you look at the safety gear builders wear.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Look, don't touch. A grown-up checks anything electric.

schedule.what: Find five dangers at home and write a safety rule for each one.

activities.record: Write five dangers and a rule for each one.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up looking at a wet bathroom floor, a loose wire near a socket, and a stool by a balcony wall.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round and spot dangers.

setup.art: A builder in a yellow helmet, bright jacket, strong boots and a harness clipped to scaffolding.
setup.caption: 2. Look at what builders wear, and why.

flow.do: Walk round the home. Look for wet floors, loose wires, sharp corners, things near a balcony wall, and heavy things on high shelves.
flow.say: Builders follow safety rules so nobody gets hurt. Let's look for places in our home where someone could get hurt.
flow.kid: Walk round with a grown-up. Find places where someone could get hurt.
flow.parent: Good finds: a stool or box near a balcony wall that a small child could climb, a wet floor, a loose plug, a heavy pot on a high shelf, a sharp corner at a child's head height. Fix anything you can straight away.
flow.context: This is the Safety Walk. Here you find dangers at home and make a rule for each one.

flow.do: Look at the picture of a builder and ask why each piece of gear is needed.
flow.say: Why does a builder wear a hard helmet? Why strong boots? Why a harness when working high up?
flow.kid: Look at the builder. Why the helmet? Why the boots? Why the harness?

check.q: Why does a builder working high up wear a harness tied to the building?
options: To carry tools
So that if they slip, the harness stops them falling
To keep warm
check.why: Falls are one of the most common causes of injury on building sites. A harness tied to something strong catches the worker if they slip.

activities.title: Who Else Builds a Home?
activities.context: In this activity you look at the homes other living beings build, and work out what problem each home solves for them.

materials.item: photos of a baya weaver nest, an ant hill, a crow's nest and a spider's web, in a book or on a phone
a notebook

activities.safety: If a crow or pigeon is nesting near your window, watch from a distance and do not touch the nest.

schedule.what: Look at four animal homes. For each, say what problem it solves.

activities.record: Draw one animal home and write what problem that home solves.

setup.art: A baya weaver nest hanging over water, its entrance tube at the bottom, a male weaver bird clinging to the nest.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a baya weaver's nest.

setup.art: A crow sitting on a nest of twigs and wires in a tree beside a block of flats.
setup.caption: 2. Look for nests near your home, from a distance.

flow.do: Look at the weaver nest photo first. Ask what danger the bird has, and how the nest helps.
flow.say: Snakes and other hunters eat eggs and chicks. So where does the baya weaver hang his nest? Where is the door?
flow.kid: Snakes eat eggs. Where does the weaver hang his nest? Where is the door?
flow.parent: The male baya weaver hangs the nest from a thin branch, often over water, with the entrance as a long tube opening downwards. Females inspect the nests and choose one. Crows in cities often build nests of twigs and even bits of wire.
flow.context: This is about animal homes. Here you see what problem each animal's home solves.

flow.do: Compare the nest with your own home.
flow.say: What does our home do that the weaver's nest also does?
flow.kid: What does your home do that the nest also does?
flow.parent: Both keep off rain and sun, keep young ones safe, and keep out hunters.

projects.title: Build a Newspaper Hut You Can Sit In
projects.context: In this two-day project you roll newspaper into strong sticks, tape them into triangles, and build a hut big enough to sit inside.

materials.item: old newspapers, about 30 double sheets
cello tape or brown packing tape
a thin stick or pencil to roll the newspaper around
an old bedsheet or dupatta, for the walls
a measuring tape

projects.safety: Build on the floor, away from the stove and lamps. Don't climb on the hut.

schedule.what: Roll 30 newspaper sticks. Tape them into triangles, and test a square of sticks against a triangle.
Join the triangles into a hut. Cover it with a sheet. Push it gently to test it, and add braces where it leans.

projects.record: Draw your hut and mark every triangle. Write where it leaned and what you did to fix it.

setup.art: A double sheet of newspaper being rolled tightly from one corner around a pencil into a long thin stick, with tape at the end.
setup.caption: 1. Roll newspaper tightly from a corner and tape the end.

setup.art: Three newspaper sticks taped into a triangle, with the tape wrapped round each corner.
setup.caption: 2. Tape the sticks into triangles.

setup.art: A tent-shaped hut of newspaper triangles on a living room floor, partly covered by a bedsheet, a child sitting inside.
setup.caption: 3. Join the triangles into a hut and cover it.

flow.do: 1. Lay a double sheet of newspaper flat. 2. Roll it tightly from one corner around a pencil. 3. Slide the pencil out and tape the end. 4. Make 30 sticks.
flow.say: We need about 30 sticks. Roll tightly, because a tight roll is much stronger than a loose one.
flow.kid: Roll newspaper tightly from one corner. Tape the end. Make 30 sticks.
flow.parent: Rolling from the corner gives a long, thin, strong stick about 80 cm long. Share the rolling. Aim for sticks of about the same length.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the newspaper hut. Here you roll newspaper into strong sticks.

flow.do: 1. Tape four sticks into a square and three into a triangle. 2. Stand each upright and push the top gently.
flow.say: Remember the card frames? Let's see if big newspaper frames behave the same way.
flow.kid: Make a big square and a big triangle. Push each one. What happens?
flow.parent: The square will lean, just like the card one. The taped corners hold a little, but still bend.

flow.do: Day 2: 1. Tape three triangles together at their sides to make a tent shape, like a tall pyramid. 2. Add more triangles until it is big enough to sit in. 3. Tape each joint firmly.
flow.say: Let's build our hut from triangles. Where will the door be?
flow.kid: Join your triangles into a hut. Leave a gap for the door.
flow.parent: A simple shape is a square base with four triangles leaning in to meet at the top, with a brace across each side of the base. Leave one side open as a door.
flow.wait: Come back to this on day 2.

flow.do: 1. Push gently on each side. 2. Where it leans, add a stick from corner to corner. 3. Cover it with the sheet and sit inside.
flow.say: Push it gently. Does it lean anywhere? What can we add to stop it?
flow.kid: Push your hut gently. If it leans, add a brace. Then go inside.

check.q: One side of your hut leans when you push it. What is the best fix?
options: Add more tape to the corners
Add a stick from one corner of that side to the opposite corner
Make the sticks longer
check.why: A stick from corner to corner, called a brace, turns the leaning square into two triangles, and triangles cannot lean. More tape helps only a little, because a taped corner can still bend.

challenges.title: The Tower That Stands in the Fan's Wind
challenges.problem: Build the tallest tower you can from newspaper and tape. It must stay standing for 30 seconds while a table fan blows on it.
constraints: Use only 10 sheets of newspaper and 1 metre of tape.
The tower must stand on its own, with nothing holding it.
Put the fan on its highest speed, 1 metre away.
general: Roll the newspaper into sticks and tape them into a tower of triangles.
Make the base wide and the top narrow, like a mobile tower.
Add braces across each side so the tower cannot lean.
creative: Make the tower a hollow tube with diagonal strips on the outside, like Fazlur Rahman Khan's John Hancock Center.
Leave gaps in the sides so the wind can pass through, as it does through a steel tower.
Fold paper into a fan shape for the walls, because folds make paper stiff.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own tower. Draw it first, build it, then test it in the fan's wind. Change one thing and test again.

flow.do: 1. Stand one rolled newspaper stick upright in front of the fan. 2. Switch the fan on.
flow.say: Let's see the problem first. What does the wind do to a single stick?
flow.kid: Stand one stick up. Turn on the fan. What happens?
flow.context: This is the Fan's Wind challenge. First you see how wind pushes a tower sideways.

flow.do: Draw three tower ideas together before building.
flow.say: Engineers draw before they build. What shapes did we learn are good at not leaning?
flow.kid: Draw three ideas for a tower. Use what you learned about triangles.

flow.do: 1. Build the best idea. 2. Measure its height. 3. Test it in the fan for 30 seconds. 4. Improve it and test again.
flow.say: Build it and test it. If it falls, look at where it bent first.
flow.kid: Build your tower. Measure it. Test it in the wind. Fix it and try again.
flow.parent: The tower often bends at a joint low down. A wider base and braces near the bottom help most.

flow.do: Ask your child what they changed and why it helped.
flow.say: What did you change after the first test? Why did it help?
flow.kid: What did you change? Why did it help?
flow.parent: A strong answer names a change, such as a wider base or a brace, and links it to the tower not leaning.

challenges.title: The Flood-Proof House
challenges.problem: Families in Assam live with floods every year. Build a small model house that stays dry when water 3 cm deep flows round it in a tray.
constraints: The house must be at least 8 cm tall.
A small paper square inside the house must stay dry.
materials: a large tray or a plastic tub
paper cups, ice-cream sticks, pencils, card, straws and tape
a small square of tissue paper
general: Raise the house on stilts, like a Mising house in Assam.
Make the floor of something that floats.
Build a wall of clay or card around the house.
creative: Make a house that floats and is tied by a string so it rises with the water.
Put stilts in upside-down paper cups so they stand firm on the tray.
Add braces between the stilts so they do not lean when water pushes them.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own flood-proof house. Pour the water in slowly, then quickly. Does your house stay dry, and stay standing?

flow.do: Look at a photo of a house on stilts in Assam during a flood.
flow.say: When the river floods, the water flows under this house. Why does the family stay dry?
flow.kid: Look at the house on stilts. Why does the family stay dry in the flood?
flow.context: This is the Flood-Proof House challenge. You design a house that stays dry in a flood.

flow.do: 1. Build a house. 2. Put the tissue inside on the floor. 3. Stand it in the tray. 4. Pour water slowly until it is 3 cm deep. 5. Check the tissue.
flow.say: Build it, then we will flood the tray. Pour slowly. Is the tissue still dry?
flow.kid: Build your house. Put the tissue inside. Flood the tray. Is the tissue dry?
flow.parent: Stilts often lean when the water pushes them. Braces between the stilts fix that. Mop up spills straight away.

flow.do: Ask what worked and what they would change.
flow.say: What kept the floor dry? What would you change for a bigger flood?
flow.kid: What kept your house dry? What would you change?
flow.parent: A strong answer explains that raising the floor above the water keeps it dry, and that stilts need braces.
