quiz.p: What does a shelter protect us from?
opts: Only from rain
Rain, sun, heat, cold, wind and danger
Only from animals
quiz.why: A shelter protects from all of these. Choosing only one leaves out the others.

quiz.p: You push a square frame of card strips sideways. What happens?
opts: It stays square
It leans and folds flat
It becomes a triangle
quiz.why: The square's corners turn like hinges, so it leans. Choosing 'stays square' usually means thinking more strips make it stronger.

quiz.p: Why can a triangle frame not lean?
opts: It is made of stronger card
To lean, one side would have to change length
It is smaller than a square
quiz.why: Three fixed lengths make only one shape. The card was the same in both frames, so the material is not the reason.

quiz.p: Ananya, a girl in Class 3, has a wobbly square frame. Where should she add a strip to stop it leaning?
opts: From one corner to the opposite corner
Along the bottom
Across the middle, side to side
quiz.why: A strip from corner to corner, a brace, makes two triangles. Along the bottom or across the middle leaves shapes that can still lean.

quiz.p: Which of these is built from many triangles?
opts: A mobile phone tower
A brick wall
A glass window
quiz.why: A mobile tower is a truss of steel triangles. A brick wall is a block, and a window is one sheet.

quiz.p: Why do many houses in Ladakh have flat mud roofs?
opts: Ladakh gets very little rain
Ladakh has no wood at all
Flat roofs keep out snakes
quiz.why: With very little rain, water rarely stands on the roof, and the flat roof is useful for drying food.

quiz.p: Families in parts of Assam build houses on bamboo stilts. Why?
opts: To see further
So floodwater can flow under the floor
To catch more wind
quiz.why: Rivers in Assam flood every year. A raised floor keeps the family and their things dry.

quiz.p: Water was poured on a flat tray and on a tray tilted on four books. What happened?
opts: Both dried at the same time
The water ran off the tilted tray fast and stayed on the flat one
The water stayed on the tilted tray
quiz.why: Water flows downhill. The steeper the slope, the faster it runs off.

quiz.p: How must roof tiles overlap to keep rain out?
opts: Each higher tile lies on top of the tile below
Each lower tile lies on top of the tile above
They should not overlap at all
quiz.why: Then water runs from one tile onto the outside of the next and never slips under an edge. In the tile test, the other way let water through.

quiz.p: Why does a builder working high up wear a harness?
opts: To look smart
So that a slip does not become a fall
To carry bricks
quiz.why: Falls are one of the biggest dangers on a building site. A harness tied to something strong catches the worker.

quiz.p: Which is a good safety rule at home?
opts: Climb on the balcony wall to see better
Leave a wet floor to dry by itself
Never climb on balcony walls or grills
quiz.why: Falls from balconies are a real danger. Wet floors should be wiped at once.

quiz.p: In an earthquake, why is a heavy roof more dangerous than a light one?
opts: Heavy roofs are pushed harder by the shaking and hurt more if they fall
Heavy roofs let rain in
Heavy roofs are hotter
quiz.why: The shaking pushes heavy things harder, and a falling heavy roof is the main danger. In Kutch in 2001, many bhungas with light roofs stood.

items.p: In the Push Test, you pushed the top of a square card frame sideways. What happened?
opts: It stayed square
It leaned into a diamond and folded flat
One strip broke
items.why: The corners of a square turn like hinges, so the square leans and folds without any strip changing length.

items.p: Which of these frames keeps its shape when pushed?
opts: A square
A rectangle
A triangle
items.why: A triangle cannot change shape unless one side changes length. Squares and rectangles can lean by turning their corners.

items.p: A strip fixed from one corner of a frame to the opposite corner, so it cannot lean, is called a ____.
items.why: A brace turns a square into two triangles.

items.p: A square frame is stronger than a triangle frame, because it has more strips.
items.why: False. In the Push Test, the square folded flat and the triangle did not. The number of strips matters less than the shape they make.

items.p: Match each house to the place it suits.
pairs: Flat mud roof and thick walls
Ladakh, cold and very little rain
Round mud house with a light roof
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each house suits the weather and dangers of its place.

items.p: Sort these building materials. Did they come from nature with little change, or were they made in a factory?
items.a: see items
items.why: Mud, bamboo, stone and grass are used almost as they are found. Glass, cement and steel are made by heating materials from nature in factories.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, says, "My card square folded, so the card must be weak." What would you tell her?
items.a: The card is not weak. The triangle was made of the same card and it did not fold. The square folds because its corners can turn, so its shape can change without any strip bending.
items.why: A strong answer uses the triangle as evidence that the material is the same, and says the shape is the reason.

items.p: Draw a square frame. Then draw one strip that stops it leaning. Colour the two triangles it makes.
items.a: A square with one diagonal from one corner to the opposite corner, with the two triangles coloured.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the brace from corner to corner, not across the middle of a side.
items.art: An empty square drawn in pencil.

items.p: Why do many houses in Assam stand on bamboo stilts?
opts: So floodwater can flow under the floor
So the house is cooler in winter
Because bamboo is too short for walls
items.why: When the river floods, water flows under the raised floor, so the family and their things stay dry.

items.p: Label the parts of this house: roof, wall, frame, brace, door.
items.why: A strong answer puts the brace across the frame from corner to corner.
items.art: A simple house drawing with its frame showing on one side, a diagonal brace in the frame, a sloping roof and a door, with five empty label lines.

items.p: On a model roof, rain runs off faster when the roof is steep.
items.why: True. Water flows downhill, so it runs off a steep roof faster. On a flat tray, it stayed in a puddle.

items.p: Why does a builder wear a hard helmet?
opts: To keep the sun off
To protect the head from falling bricks or tools
So others can tell who the builder is
items.why: Things can fall from above on a building site. A hard helmet protects the head.

items.p: Put these steps of the Push Test in the right order.
items: Join the strips into a frame
Measure how far the corner moved
a: Join the strips into a frame
Measure how far the corner moved
items.why: You build the frame, hold the bottom still, then push and measure.

items.p: Name two things a shelter protects us from. Then name one animal that builds a shelter.
items.a: For example: rain and hot sun. A baya weaver builds a hanging nest.
items.why: A strong answer gives two real dangers and one real animal home.

items.p: A frame made of many triangles joined together is called a ____.
items.why: Trusses are used in roofs, towers and bridges.

items.p: In the tile test, the tissue under roof B got wet, but the tissue under roof A stayed dry. Explain why, using the word 'overlap'.
items.a: On roof A, each higher tile overlaps the one below it, so water runs from the top of one tile onto the outside of the next and off the edge. On roof B, each lower tile overlaps the one above, so water runs into the edge of each tile, under it, and through the gap.
items.why: A strong answer follows the water down the roof and says where it got in.

items.p: A family in Chennai is building a new house.

views.says: Let's use concrete and steel. It is strong, it can have two floors, and it will not wash away in a cyclone.
Let's use brick with a jaali wall and a tiled roof, like Laurie Baker's houses. It stays cool without an AC and uses fewer bricks.
It doesn't matter which material we use, as long as the frame has braces and the roof is not too heavy.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with a fact, such as concrete's strength, a jaali wall's breeze, or the Push Test showing braces matter. It then admits a fair point from another side, because each choice has real costs and gains.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Builders and architects really disagree about this.

items.p: Mythili, a girl in Class 4, adds a strip across her square frame, from the middle of the top to the middle of the bottom. Will it stop the square leaning?
opts: Yes, any extra strip stops leaning
No, it makes two smaller squares, which can still lean
Only if the strip is thicker
items.why: A strip from the middle of the top to the middle of the bottom makes two smaller rectangles, not triangles. Rectangles still lean. The brace must go from corner to corner.

items.p: Draw a side view of a roof with four tiles overlapping the right way. Add arrows to show where rain runs.
items.a: Four tiles in a slope, each higher tile lying over the top of the one below, with arrows running down over each tile and off the bottom edge.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the higher tile on top every time, and the arrows never go under a tile.
items.art: A sloping line for a roof with space to draw tiles on it.

items.p: In the Kutch earthquake of 2001, many bhungas with light roofs stood. Why is a light roof safer in an earthquake?
opts: A light roof is cheaper
If a light roof falls, it is far less likely to hurt people, and shaking pushes light things less
A light roof keeps the house cool
items.why: The shaking ground pushes heavy things harder, and a falling heavy roof is the main danger. A light roof both moves less and hurts less if it falls.

items.p: Houses in Ladakh have flat roofs, but houses in Kerala have steep roofs. Explain why, using what you saw in the Rain on the Roof test.
items.a: In the test, water stayed in a puddle on the flat tray but ran off the steep tray in seconds. Kerala gets very heavy rain, so it needs steep roofs to shed water. Ladakh gets very little rain, so a flat roof is fine and can be used for drying food.
items.why: A strong answer uses the test results, then links each roof to each place's rain.

items.p: Sort these. Will each one keep its shape when pushed, or lean?
items: a gate with a diagonal plank
a gate with no diagonal plank
a ladder leaning on a wall, with the floor
a tall rectangle shelf with no back
items.a: see items
items.why: Anything split completely into triangles keeps its shape. A shape with four or more sides and no braces can lean.

items.p: In an earthquake, the ground pushes a building mostly sideways, not only down.
items.why: True. Shaking moves the ground from side to side, so walls and frames are pushed sideways, like your push on the card square.

items.p: Label the parts of a baya weaver's nest: branch, nest room, entrance tube, water below.
items.why: A strong answer shows the entrance tube at the bottom, which makes it hard for snakes to get in.
items.art: A hanging grass nest with four empty label lines.

items.p: Laurie Baker's rat-trap bond lays bricks on their edges, with a gap inside the wall. What does the gap do?
opts: Saves bricks and keeps the room cooler
Lets rats live in the wall
Makes the wall heavier
items.why: The air gap means fewer bricks are needed, and still air slows heat coming through the wall. The name comes from the shape of the brick pattern, not from rats.

items.p: A frame that keeps its shape when pushed is called ____.
items.why: Rigid means it does not lean or fold. A triangle is rigid.

items.p: Meera, a girl in Class 3, says the pandal in the story leaned because Arun's knots were loose. Is she right? What really happened?
items.a: No. Not one knot came undone and no pole broke. The pandal leaned because its frame was made of squares, which can lean when their corners turn. The cross poles made triangles and stopped it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the story's evidence and names the missing triangles.

items.p: Put these roofs in order, from the one where 4 spoons of water stopped dripping first to the one where it stayed longest.
items.why: The steeper the roof, the faster the water ran off. On the flat tray it stayed in a puddle.

items.p: Match each safety gear to why a builder wears it.
pairs: protects the head from falling things
protect the feet from nails and glass
stops a fall when working high up
helps truck and crane drivers see the worker
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each piece of gear stops one common way of getting hurt.

items.p: Thilaga, a girl in Class 3, wants a light frame for a balcony tent. Which one will stay up best in the wind?
opts: Four sticks in a square
Sticks in triangles, with a brace on each side
One tall stick in the middle
items.why: Triangles and braces stop the frame leaning in a sideways push from the wind. A square can fold, and one stick can tip over.

items.p: Many people think a heavier, thicker wall is always safer. Using what you learned about earthquakes, what would you test to find out if that is true?
items.a: Build two small model houses on a tray, one with a heavy roof of clay or books and one with a light card roof, both with the same walls. Shake the tray the same way and see which falls first. Repeat three times.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing, the weight, keeps everything else the same, and repeats the test.

items.p: A town is being rebuilt after an earthquake.

views.says: Build new houses of concrete with steel rods, tested to the earthquake rules.

views.who: Gauri, a mason who builds bhungas
views.says: Build round mud houses with light roofs, as our families did. They stood when new buildings fell.

items.ask: Which builder would you choose for your family's house? Give a reason from this unit. Then say what the other builder has right.
items.a: A strong answer chooses one side with a real reason, for example that the bhungas stood in 2001, or that well-built concrete can be tall and strong. It then admits a fair point: how well a house is built matters more than the material.
items.why: Both views are held by real experts. A strong answer shows it understands the trade-off.

items.p: Fazlur Rahman Khan put huge diagonal braces on the outside of the John Hancock Center in Chicago. What did they do?
opts: They held up the windows
They made giant triangles, so the tower did not lean in the wind, using less steel
They made the building heavier, so wind could not push it
items.why: The diagonals made giant triangles across the outside walls. Triangles cannot lean, so the whole building stayed stiff, and it used about as much steel for each floor as a 50-storey building.

items.p: Design a balcony shelter for a pigeon or a crow, using only sticks and string. Draw it and mark every triangle in red.
items.a: Any shelter whose frame is split into triangles, with a roof sloping to shed rain, and an opening for the bird.
items.why: A strong design uses triangles or braces in every side and a sloping roof, and thinks about what the bird needs.
items.art: A blank box with a balcony grill drawn at the bottom.

items.p: A Toda hut in the Nilgiris has a very small door. The Nilgiris are cool and misty. What problem do you think the small door solves for the family?
items.a: A small door lets less cold air in and less warm air out, so the hut stays warmer. It is also easy to close.
items.why: A strong answer links the door to keeping warmth in, in a cool place. It is fine to say this is a guess.

items.p: A frame with six sides leans when pushed. What is the smallest number of strips you need to add so it cannot lean?
items.why: Three strips from one corner to three far corners split a six-sided shape into four triangles. With fewer, a four-sided part is left, and it can lean.

items.p: In a city, building tall blocks of flats lets many families live on a small piece of land.
items.why: True. Building upwards puts many homes on the same ground, which matters where land is scarce and costly.

items.p: Your square frame and your triangle frame used the same card and the same pins. What does that show about where a frame's strength comes from?
items.a: It shows strength does not come only from the material. The shape and the way the parts are joined matter too. The same card was floppy as a square and firm as a triangle.
items.why: A strong answer uses the Push Test as evidence and separates the material from the shape.

items.p: Sort these homes by the main danger they are built to handle.
items: a bamboo house on stilts in Assam
a Toda hut with a small door
a thatched house with a steep roof
items.a: see items
items.why: Each home's shape answers the biggest problem of its place.

items.p: Label this tower: wide base, narrow top, brace, triangle.
items.why: A strong answer shows why each part helps the tower stand in the wind.
items.art: A tall steel tower drawing, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, with crossed diagonals, and four empty label lines.

items.p: Why do roofs in Ladakh stay flat, though flat roofs would leak in Kerala?
opts: Ladakh gets very little rain, so water rarely stands on the roof
Ladakh has stronger mud
Snow never falls in Ladakh
items.why: Ladakh is a cold desert with very little rain, so a flat roof rarely holds water. Some snow falls, but it is light. In Kerala, heavy rain would stand on a flat mud roof and soak in.

items.p: The baya weaver hangs his nest over water, with the door at the bottom. What problem does he have, and how does the nest solve it?
items.a: His problem is that snakes and other hunters eat eggs and chicks. The nest hangs from a thin branch, often over water, which a snake finds hard to reach. The door is a long tube opening downwards, which makes it very hard to climb in.
items.why: A strong answer names the bird's problem first, then how each feature of the nest helps.

items.p: The most common causes of death in an earthquake are buildings and roofs ____ on people.
items.why: Most people are hurt by falling buildings, not by the shaking itself. That is why light roofs and braces save lives.

items.p: Put these in order, from the frame that leans most to the one that leans least when pushed.
items: a square with one loose, wobbly brace
a: a square with one loose, wobbly brace
items.why: A square leans freely. A loose brace stops some leaning but lets the frame wobble. A triangle with firm joints barely moves.

items.p: The Tao Te Ching says it is the empty space inside a room that makes it useful. What do the walls and the frame do for that space?
items.a: The walls and frame hold their shape and keep out rain, wind and danger, so that the empty space inside stays open and safe for us to live in.
items.why: A strong answer links the frame's job to the space it protects. There is no single right answer.

applications: Roofs of houses, sheds, railway stations and factories are held up by trusses made of triangles.
Mobile phone towers, electricity pylons and cranes are tall frames of steel triangles.
Steel railway and road bridges, such as the Howrah Bridge in Kolkata, use triangles along their sides.
Gates, ladders, folding stools and shelf brackets use braces and triangles so they do not wobble.
Tall buildings use diagonal braces or a very stiff core to stand up to wind and earthquakes.
Wedding and festival pandals are tied with cross poles so the wind cannot push them over.
Sloping roofs and overlapping tiles keep homes dry in the monsoon.
Houses on stilts keep families dry in flood areas.

open_questions.q: How exactly do baya weavers learn to weave such good nests?
open_questions.why_open: Young males build better nests with practice, and females choose among nests. How much is learned and how much they are born knowing is still being studied.

open_questions.q: What is the best way to build homes that are cheap, cool and safe in earthquakes, for millions of families?
open_questions.why_open: Engineers, architects and builders still argue about it, because the answer depends on the place, the money, the materials and how carefully the house is built.

open_questions.q: Can we predict exactly when and where an earthquake will happen?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can say which areas are at risk, but nobody can yet say the day or hour of an earthquake.

open_questions.q: Could houses one day be grown, from fungi or plants, instead of built?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are testing building blocks made from fungi and plant fibres. Nobody knows yet whether they will last as long as brick.

jokes.a: It kept feeling a bit off-balance.

jokes.j: What did the triangle say to the square?
Why are triangles never pushed around?
What did the roof say to the rain?
Why did the house go to school?
What kind of music do builders like?
Why did the brick feel lonely?

jokes.j: What did one wall say to the other wall?
jokes.a: I'll meet you at the corner.

jokes.j: Why was the tile so calm in the monsoon?

jokes.j: What did the brace say to the gate?

maths.problem: In the Push Test, the top corner of the square moved 12 cm. The top corner of the triangle moved half a centimetre. How many centimetres further did the square's corner move?
maths.explain: 12 cm take away half a centimetre is 11 and a half centimetres. The square leaned more than 20 times as far as the triangle.
maths.context: This is about the Push Test, where you pushed card frames sideways and measured how far the top corner moved.

chart.title: How far the top corner moved

maths.why_maths: Taking one number from the other shows exactly how much more one frame leaned.

maths.problem: Divya, a girl in Class 3, wants to build 4 card triangles. Each triangle needs 3 strips. How many strips does she need?
maths.explain: 4 triangles with 3 strips each is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. Or 4 times 3 is 12.
maths.context: This is about making card frames like the ones in the Push Test.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying tells you how many strips to cut before you start, so you don't run out.

maths.problem: A square frame needs 4 strips. A square with a brace needs 5 strips. A triangle needs 3. How many strips do you need to make one of each?
maths.explain: 4 + 5 + 3 = 12. You can add the 5 and the 3 first to make 8, then add 4 to make 12.
maths.context: This is about the three frames in the Push Test.
maths.why_maths: Adding up first lets you cut the right number of strips for the whole test.

maths.problem: In the Rain on the Roof test, water stopped dripping after 4 seconds on four books, 20 seconds on one book, and still stood in a puddle after 60 seconds on the flat tray. How many times as long did the water take on one book as on four books?
maths.explain: 20 seconds divided by 4 seconds is 5. So the gentler slope took 5 times as long. Check: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20.
maths.context: This is about Rain on the Roof. You poured 4 spoons of water on a tray at three slopes and timed how long until it stopped dripping.

chart.title: Seconds until the water stopped dripping

maths.why_maths: Dividing tells us how many times faster a steep roof sheds rain, which helps a builder choose a slope.

maths.problem: An ordinary wall needs about 100 bricks. A rat-trap bond wall of the same size needs about a quarter fewer. About how many bricks does the rat-trap wall need?
maths.explain: A quarter of 100 is 25, because 100 shared into 4 equal parts is 25 each. 100 take away 25 is 75.
maths.context: This is about Laurie Baker's rat-trap bond, a way of laying bricks on their edges with a gap inside the wall.
maths.why_maths: Working out a quarter shows how many bricks, and how much money, a new design can save.

maths.problem: A pentagon frame has 5 sides. Two braces from one corner split it into triangles. How many triangles are there? Draw it to check.
maths.explain: Two strips from one corner reach the two far corners. They cut the five-sided shape into 3 triangles. A shape with 6 sides needs 3 braces and makes 4 triangles. The number of triangles is always 2 less than the number of sides.
maths.context: This is about the Lean or Stand game, where frames with more sides need braces to keep their shape.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you say how many braces any frame needs without drawing it.

roots.context: We have tested frames, roofs and tiles, and met houses from all over India. Now we ask what building a shelter tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your square frame folded flat at one push, but your triangle frame kept its shape. Both were made of the same card strips and pins. Three sides of fixed length fit together in only one shape, while four sides can lean into many. So a roof or tower stays firm because its parts form triangles.
deep_truth.habit: We usually think a building is strong because its material is strong, thick or heavy. But your two frames used the same strips, and one folded while the other held. How the parts are joined decides as much as what they are made of.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Push Test, the top corner of the square moved many centimetres and the square folded flat. The triangle's corner moved less than one centimetre. One diagonal strip across the square stopped it leaning too.

three.who_am_i: Your skeleton is your frame. When you stand with your feet apart, your legs and the floor make a triangle, and you are much harder to push over.
three.what_is_life: Every living being needs shelter. A baya weaver weaves a hanging nest, ants dig rooms under the soil, and people build houses.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything that stands is pushed all the time, by its own weight, by wind and by the ground. It stays standing because its parts push back.

roots.thread: A Toda hut, a Kerala tiled house, a Ladakh mud house and a block of flats in Chennai look nothing alike. They are made of grass, clay, mud or concrete, by different people, for different weather. Yet under every one is the same simple rule: a frame stays firm when its parts make triangles. One plain fact about three sides, found again and again by builders who never met, takes shape as thousands of different homes.

teachings.teaching: We cut out doors and windows to make a room. It is the empty space inside that makes the room useful.
teachings.link: Your frames and a house's walls hold their shape so that an empty space can stay open inside. We build the walls, but we live in the space they hold.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha spoke of seeking the builder of a house. He said that its rafters were broken and its ridge-pole was shattered, so that house would not be built again.
teachings.link: The Buddha used a house of rafters and a ridge-pole as a picture of the self. A house is only parts held together at their joints. When the joints and beams fail, there is no house left, only poles.

science.text: A triangle of fixed sides cannot change shape, so trusses made of triangles hold big loads with little material. This is used in roofs, cranes, towers and bridges.
How well traditional mud houses stand up to earthquakes, compared with concrete houses, depends a lot on how each one is built. Engineers are still studying this.

other_view.who: Le Corbusier, a famous architect, in his book Vers une architecture, which means Towards an Architecture (1923)
other_view.view: He wrote that a house is a machine for living in. In this view, a house is a useful tool, like a car, built as well and as cheaply as possible. It carries no deeper meaning about life, and reading one into it is our own idea.

practice.title: Stand like a triangle
practice.say: Stand up with your feet close together. I will press very gently on your shoulder. Did you wobble? Now stand with your feet wide apart. Your legs and the floor make a triangle. I will press again, just as gently. Did you wobble now? Close your eyes and take five slow breaths. Feel the floor pushing up through your feet. Feel how steady you are.
practice.kid: Stand with your feet together. Lean a little to one side. Do you wobble? Now stand with your feet wide apart. Your legs and the floor make a triangle. Lean again. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly five times. Feel the floor holding you up.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home, with the materials listed. Card from a cereal box is stiff enough. Thin paper bends and spoils the Push Test, so the step says to use thicker card. Split pins must be left loose, or a pressed-tight joint makes even the square stiff for a moment. Twist ties or knotted thread are the home alternative. The square's corner moves 10 to 14 cm, and the triangle's less than 1 cm, which is easy to see on a ruler. In Rain on the Roof, a tray with a high rim holds water even when tilted, so the step asks for a flat tray, a plastic file cover or a rimless plate. In the tile test, milk packets are thin and easy to cut and tape, and the slit in the card makes leaks show clearly on the tissue. The newspaper hut needs about 30 tightly rolled sticks, which takes two people about 25 minutes. Nothing in the spine needs a garden or a park.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1960s, buildings were getting taller, and engineers had a problem. A tall building is pushed sideways by the wind, like a tree. Most engineers thought the answer was a thick skeleton of columns and beams with very stiff joints. But each extra floor then needed more and more steel, so very tall buildings cost far too much. Fazlur Rahman Khan, an engineer born in Dhaka in 1929, thought about it differently. He worked in Chicago, in the United States, with the architect Bruce Graham. Khan saw that the outside walls could work like one stiff hollow tube. For the John Hancock Center, a 100-storey tower finished in 1969, he put huge diagonal steel braces across the outside, making giant triangles. The triangles stopped the building leaning in the wind. The tower used about as much steel for each floor as an ordinary 50-storey building. The old idea, that height needed ever thicker skeletons, was shown wrong. Triangles, placed well, did the work instead.
how_we_found_out.who: Fazlur Rahman Khan, an engineer born in Dhaka, with the architect Bruce Graham, in Chicago
how_we_found_out.when: The 1960s. The John Hancock Center was finished in 1969.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Engineers thought that a taller building needed a thicker and heavier skeleton of columns and stiff joints, so very tall towers would cost too much steel. Khan showed that big diagonal braces making triangles on the outside could hold the building firm against wind with far less steel.
